cases.situation: Zoe started three weeks ago. She has no full month of records yet, so Decide uses her quick estimates (pay £2,500, bills £1,000, everyday £300). Besides the estimates, Decide counts what she has recorded: £1,280 in her Main current account on 22 November, a card with £400 on it at 24.9% whose £25 minimum is due on 28 November (it is not one of her bills), and £300 in a savings account she marked as her safety net. She has not recorded an overdraft limit on Main, or any loan. Pay of £2,500 lands on 1 December. She is looking at £1,150. It is bought on 22 November 2026 (today), paid in one go. Monthly spending from the quick estimates: bills £1,000 and everyday spending £300 (£200 of it on essentials).
cases.why: Quick estimates never stand alone: what she has recorded is counted too (D-43). The rest of her £300 everyday estimate is £80, so her £1,280 leaves £1,200 free; the £25 card minimum on 28 November comes before payday, so £1,200 - £25 - £1,150 = £25 left. With no full month of records, the floor comes from her estimates: a tenth of £1,000 bills + £300 everyday spending = £130, and £25 is under it, so the answer is "Fits, but tight" (D-40). Tight leads; the safety-net line shows as a fact, because her £300 net is below its £1,225 starter size (£1,000 bills + £25 card minimum + £200 essential everyday spending, D-51): "Your safety net has £300 of its £1,225. 1 month is a start; 3 to 6 months is common." The card shows as a fact (about £8.30 a month in interest at 24.9%). The sentence says it is based on her quick estimates, a fact says "No full month of records yet.", and because no overdraft limit or loan is recorded the answer asks, without blocking: "No loan or overdraft is recorded. Do you have one?" with "Add it" and "None" (ask, don't block).

cases.situation: It is 1 December and Lucy is offline. Her records last synced on 29 November, so December has no records yet. November was a full, usual month that left $1,000, and that $1,000 is still in her everyday account. December's pay of $3,000 is due today and has not arrived yet. Her safety net is full ($1,700). She is looking at a $500 purchase. It is bought on 1 December 2026 (today), paid in one go. A usual month: pay $3,000, bills $1,200 and everyday spending $800 ($500 of it on essentials).
cases.why: Last month's records are fresh (2 days old), so Decide answers from them instead of asking for more: December is expected to leave $1,000, like a usual month, and $1,000 - $500 = $500. The sentence says "Offline. Using records up to Nov 29."
cases.plannerNote: D-45 (verify before building), checked 2026-11-02. Mostly already happens. (1) Server: the daily materialise_recurring job (migration 20260926000400) writes every occurrence of a recurring bill or pay series through the end of next month (recurring_horizon) as a "pending" row, which the app labels "Expected"; it stays pending until the user confirms it paid or received. So when Lucy last synced on 29 November, December's Expected rows were already in her cache. (2) Engine: v3 month/thisMonth.ts counts each live bill occurrence in the month as due until a paid line settles it (month/settle.ts: a pending line never settles, and a due date passing settles nothing); month/incomeProfile.ts counts pay series at their dates (dropped only after the missed-pay grace days) and other pending income only when the user marked it expected. Gaps for the planner: everyday spending that is not a recurring series does not roll over as rows (the engine uses the typical month instead); and fixture.ts does not model pending rows, so this case cannot assert the rollover yet.
